newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia traders expect fattening for lean Brent/Dubai.
newsitem.headline: Asia traders expect fattening for lean Brent/Dubai.

text.p: An abnormally narrow Brent/Dubai differential, responsible for the major influx of West African crude oil into Asia in recent weeks, may not have much life left, crude oil traders said on Monday.
"The current differential is simply too low," said one trader with a Japanese refiner.
"There could be a correction in order," he added.
The discount of Asian benchmark Dubai crude to North Sea bellwether Dated Brent is the primary trigger for the eastward flow of Brent-linked crudes into Asia.

Current Brent/Dubai differentials of 90 cents to one dollar, compared with levels in the $2.50 range in February, have made Brent-related West African barrels an especially lucrative alternative to Dubai-linked Asian crudes for regional refiners.

West African crude deliveries into Asia amounted to some 855,000 bpd in the first quarter of this year, a five percent uptick over last year's levels, according to London-based tanker broker Simpson, Spence & Young.
And volumes fixed in April look to have exceeded that level, crude oil traders said.

China, which typically plays a waiting game for favourable price swings then buys in large volumes, fixed an estimated 4.5 million barrels of West-African Palanca, Zafiro, and Cabinda grades for first-half June loading, traders said.

But traders said rumours of relative weakness in Asian wet markets and the prospect of a recovery in North Sea markets may see the Brent/Dubai differential widen to more representative levels in the weeks to come.
"We are hearing there is an oil major stuck with about four or five cargoes of Dubai, so there may be some softening on this end of the spread," said one Asian trader.
Traders also estimated that about two million to three million barrels of Abu Dhabi grades, including Murban, Umm Shaif, and Lower Zakum, were still looking for buyers in Asia.
Meanwhile, a perceived tightening of Atlantic basin markets could portend a relative North Sea comeback.
"What we're seeing is...the perception that West African flows east have dried things up in the west," a trader with a European major said.
"That's good news for Brent," he said.
Traders were careful to point out that in the long-term, West African shipments into Asia were likely to become more than just a factor of the Brent/Dubai differential.
A lack of requisite refinery sophistication will gradually increase Asia's reliance on the lower-sulphur West African grades in light of tightening Asian oil product specifications, they said.

While traders said it was premature to link Beijing's June implementation of a ban on leaded gasoline in the capital city with China's recent prominence in the West African market, the change could bode well in the future for West African marketers, whose sweet grades are well-suited to unleaded gasoline production.
China plans to ban the use of leaded gasoline by 2000.
South Korea, which takes approximately 150,000 bpd, or 19 percent of total West African crude east, also leans on the sweet grades as a short term fix to its longer term refinery upgrading mandate.
